outcome_verbatim: The employment rates are calculated as the percentage of participants over the total of each group that obtains at least one job in the study period fixed (8-months and 12-months).
source_locator: Results, p. 307 ('More clients in the CR + IPS group worked at 8 and 12 months (52.2% and 60.9%, respectively) than IPS (29.2% and 37.5%, p = .023 and p = .025, respectively)'); Figure 3, p. 307; group denominators from Table 4 column headers, p. 308
notes: Printed value: 52.2% of the 23 completers in this arm obtained at least one job by 8 months. NO NUMERATOR RECOVERABLE. The paper prints the employment rate only as a percentage of the group (Results p. 307 and Figure 3 p. 307); Table 4 (p. 308) reports mean number of jobs per individual, mean weekly hours and mean hourly wage, and no employment count appears anywhere in the article. The denominator IS printed (Table 4 column headers, p. 308), so multiplying it by the percentage would give a whole number, but that is exactly the back-calculation forbidden by extraction_v3 rule 1 and codebook rule 2, so n_employed is left blank. | CONSTRUCT: paid_competitive, not paid_any. The intervention is IPS, whose stated aim is competitive employment ("the aim of competitive employment with individual and rapid search jobs", p. 294); the discussion describes the outcome as "the achievement of competitive employment" (p. 309) and the study counts "the number of competitive jobs" (p. 304). | ASCERTAINMENT: any_time_during_followup, not point prevalence. The rate counts anyone who "obtains at least one job in the study period" and the paper calls these "Cumulative work rates" (p. 304). | This result cannot enter the primary pool on four independent grounds: employment-related selection at recruitment, an allocated trial arm rather than a whole cohort, a competitive-only construct, and cumulative rather than point ascertainment. | MODERATORS: no mean age is printed, only age bands (18-35, 36-45, 46-65) in Table 1, p. 301. source_locator: Table 2, p. 482, row 'Employment/occupation'; subscale definition at Methods, 2.4 Outcome measures, p. 478
notes: NO NUMERATOR EXISTS. The paper prints only a subscale mean: baseline 1.81 (SD 2.46), five-year follow-up 4.46 (SD 2.20) on a 0-10 scale (Table 2, p. 482). outcome_verbatim: People were categorized yearly based on their main activity or source of income from 2 years before to 5 years after date of first diagnosis. The starting point was categorization by Statistics Sweden, where people were categorized as employed or not employed based on income. Alternative activities and sources of income were evaluated by the number of days of receipt of social security benefits full- or part-time (including SA, parental leave, and DP) and the number of days registered as unemployed; people were assigned to the occupational activity generating income for more than 6 months yearly.
source_locator: Figure 1, p. 942 ('Development of main occupational activity of persons with first-episode nonaffective psychosis, from 2 calendar years before to 5 years after first diagnosis'); the year-1 and year-5 values are restated in Results, Sample Characteristics, p. 940; construct definition at Methods, Other Measures, pp. 939-940
conflict_note: UNRESOLVED: the base of the Figure 1 percentages is contradicted by the reported follow-up structure. The Figure 1 footnote (p. 942) states "N=21,551" for a series running to 5 years after first diagnosis, but cohort accrual ran to 2016 while data linkage ended 31 December 2016 (Methods, p. 940) and the median follow-up was 4.8 years (IQR 2.2-7.7, Results p. 940), so a large part of the cohort cannot have any year-5 observation and some cannot have a year-1 observation either. Separately, follow-up is stated to end at "death, emigration, DP, or the end of data linkage" (Methods, p. 940), yet disability pension appears in Figure 1 as a rising occupational category reaching 27.3% at year 5, so the occupational-activity series must use a different and unstated at-risk definition from the survival analysis. The two accounts cannot both be right, and which one holds determines what the printed percentages are percentages OF. Blocked from every synthesis pending an author reply. Candidate resolution (mine, not an authority, so the status stays unresolved under extraction_v3 rule 14): the occupational series is probably computed on the shrinking number under observation in each year, which would make N=21,551 a cohort size printed in a figure footnote rather than the denominator of its percentages.
notes: Printed value: 19.5% employed at 1 year after diagnosis. NO COUNT IS PRINTED for this or any other year, and none is recoverable: the only denominator offered is the figure footnote's N=21,551, which the methods contradict (see conflict_note). Nothing is read off the plotted bars; the percentages above are the figure's own printed data labels, two of which are repeated verbatim in the running text. FULL PRINTED SERIES (Figure 1, p. 942, 'Employed' row): 32.0% at 2 years before diagnosis, 30.5% at 1 year before, 22.2% in the diagnosis year, then 19.5%, 22.1%, 22.9%, 23.9% and 25.1% at years 1 to 5 after diagnosis. Years 3 and 4 are not given their own rows because year 3 (36 months) falls in no prespecified band and year 4 (48 months) is further from the 5-year landmark than year 5. | ANALYSIS-LEVEL SELECTION: 5,144 people already on disability pension at first diagnosis were excluded from the cohort (Methods, p. 940). Disability pension in Sweden is granted when work capacity is permanently reduced, so this removes precisely those least able to work and raises every employment percentage the paper prints by an unknown amount. Recorded as analysis_selection_status = selected with reason analytic_restriction on the arm row, following the precedent set for mihaljevicpeles2016. | CONSTRUCT is paid_intensity_threshold, NOT paid_any. 'Employed' here is a mutually exclusive MAIN-ACTIVITY category assigned to whoever generated income from that activity for more than 6 months of the year, so anyone in paid work for a smaller part of the year, or whose dominant income came from benefits, is counted elsewhere. The report's own Table 1 shows the two constructs differ: 35.4% had 'any income from work during previous calendar year' at cohort entry against 32.0% classified as employed two years before diagnosis. | ASCERTAINMENT is period_prevalence over a 12-month window, not point prevalence. | FOLLOW-UP: 'Time point 0 refers to the year of first psychosis diagnosis' (Figure 1 footnote, p. 942), so the timepoints are whole calendar years indexed to each person's own diagnosis year. That is measured from cohort entry, hence since_baseline, but elapsed time at 'year 1' varies across roughly 0-24 months depending on where in the diagnosis year the diagnosis fell. Raised as an author query. | MODERATORS: n_female is the exact complement of the printed male count (13,070 of 21,551, Table 1, p. 941), and Table 1's footnote states that education was the only variable with missing data, so the complement is exact. n_post_secondary uses 'High (>12 years)' education 4,508 of 21,551; note that 2,604 have unknown education, so the proportion among those with known education is higher than 20.9%. n_employed_baseline is 'Any income from work during previous calendar year' 7,634 of 21,551 (Table 1, p. 941), which is a PRE-baseline period-prevalence count and the only recoverable employment count in the report. | The paper's own estimand, an adjusted within-subject hazard ratio for sickness absence or disability pension during antipsychotic use versus nonuse (aHR=0.65, 95% CI 0.59-0.72), is not an employment outcome of this review and is not extracted as one; work disability is not employment. That within-subject effect would take ROBINS-I; the results extracted here are whole-cohort prevalences and take JBI, per SAP section 8.

outcome_verbatim: The PSP uses 4 subscales to assess problems in specific social functioning domains: (1) Social useful activities including study and work (SUA) ... Higher subscale scores reflect more problems.
source_locator: Table 4, p. 651 ('Psychosocial functioning at baseline and at 12-mo follow-up for the 3 study groups'), row 'Work and study' within this migration group; subscale definition at Methods, 2.3.4 Psychosocial functioning, p. 648
notes: NO NUMERATOR EXISTS. The paper prints only a mean severity-of-problems score on the PSP work-and-study subscale: baseline 2.39, 12 months 2.11 on a 0-4 range where HIGHER means MORE problems (P = .113). Nobody in this report is classified as employed or not employed, so there is no count to recover and no author query could produce one from what was measured; only a re-analysis of the raw PSP items could. | CONSTRUCT: the subscale is 'Social useful activities including study and work', which combines paid work with study and with other socially useful activity, so even a count would have been vocational_activity and never paid_any. | ASCERTAINMENT unclear: no recall window is stated for the PSP. | MODERATORS: Table 1 (p. 649) prints 'N (% male)' as 46 (80%), giving a male percentage but no male or female COUNT and no female percentage, so n_female and perc_female are both left blank rather than derived from a percentage. Education is given as mean years completed, not as a proportion with post-secondary education. 'Annual income (x 1000)' is a group mean in thousands, not an employment measure. | The three migration groups are a post-hoc split of ONE recruited sample of 162 and are coded as subgroup arms under D12.5, not as separate cohorts. | The sample is defined by completing both the baseline and the 12-month assessment, so the number referred and diagnosed over the recruitment period is never reported and n_entered cannot be filled.

outcome_verbatim: For the employment variable year 13, income above 100,000 Swedish kronor (SEK) (approximately 10,000 euro) was used as a cut-off for assignment as "employed".
source_locator: Table 1, p. 378 (row 'Cohort n = 161', column 'Employment year 13': '42% (67 av 161)'); restated in Results 3.5, p. 378; construct definition at Methods, 2.3 Late outcome analyses, p. 376
notes: QUANTIFIABLE: 67 of 161. NOT paid_any. Employment is defined solely by an annual income threshold of 100,000 SEK from employment during the year, so everyone in paid work earning less than that is counted as not employed. That is a threshold-defined construct under D12.3a and it must never substitute for paid_any. | ASCERTAINMENT is period_prevalence over a calendar year (2009 for those included in 1996, 2010 for those included in 1997), not point prevalence. | DENOMINATORS: 175 entered; 3 could not be retrieved from the registers and 1 had incomplete data probably from international migration; 10 died before year 13, giving 165 alive and 161 with complete records for 2009-2010 (Methods, 2.3, p. 376). | FOLLOW-UP: year 13 is anchored to each individual's own inclusion year, not to a shared calendar end date, so this is since_baseline rather than calendar_end_common; 156 months falls in the 108-months-and-above horizon either way. | MODERATORS: '55% of the cases were males' (Results 3.1, p. 378) with no count and no stated denominator (175 or 161), so neither n_female nor perc_female is recorded. Table 1 gives 'High school exam 78%, (122 of 157)'; a Swedish high-school (gymnasium) exam is upper secondary, not post-secondary, so perc_post_secondary is left blank rather than set to 78. No baseline employment proportion is reported; the years 1 to 5 employment measure was the Strauss-Carpenter scale and the paper itself warns that it is not comparable with the year-13 register measure (Discussion, p. 379). | The cohort's diagnostic listing in Results 3.2 (p. 376) accounts for only 153 of the 161 cases; see inconsistencies.md. That contradiction concerns the diagnostic breakdown, not this employment result, whose text and Table 1 values agree exactly, so conflict_status is none.

outcome_verbatim: 86 cases (53%) had any income and 67 cases (42%) had an income above 100 000 SEK year 13.
source_locator: Results 3.5, p. 378, first sentence of the second paragraph
notes: THE NEARLY-LOST RESULT OF THIS BATCH, RECORDED BUT NOT CLAIMED. 86 of 161 is a printed count on a printed denominator, so it is quantifiable; what it counts is not established. The sentence pairs 'any income' with 'an income above 100 000 SEK', which reads as any EMPLOYMENT income against employment income above the threshold, and on that reading 86/161 would be the paid_any numerator for this cohort at 13 years. But the same paper describes LISA as including 'data on income from employment, payments from sickness benefits and of student aides' (Methods, 2.3, p. 376), so 'any income' may equally mean income from any of those three sources, which is not employment at all. The report never defines the term, it appears nowhere else in the article, and neither Table 1 nor Figure 3 carries it. Coded outcome_construct = unclear under the codebook rule that an undefined construct takes `unclear` and keeps its wording; it therefore enters no pool. Promoting it to paid_any would put an unverified numerator into the primary estimand, which is the error this batch exists to avoid. An author reply on this single word would settle it; see unresolved_queries.md. | MODERATORS: '55% of the cases were males' (Results 3.1, p. 378) with no count and no stated denominator (175 or 161), so neither n_female nor perc_female is recorded. outcome_verbatim: The economic incomes included in the follow-up were salary from work on the labour market and four kinds of allowances: financial support from social services, sickness benefit, disability pension, and unemployment benefit.
source_locator: Table 3, p. 923 ('Proportion (%) of persons in the institutional recovery group vs the ongoing experiences of institutionalisation group with income from different sources'), row 'Salary', column 'Year 10'; subgroup sizes from Table 1, p. 921; income definition from Method, p. 921
notes: NO NUMERATOR RECOVERABLE. Table 3 prints 60% with income from salary at year 10 for this subgroup (persons without any contact with psychiatric or social institutional (in-patient or 24/7 housing accommodation) and community-based care (medical, psychotherapeutic or home support) for the last five consecutive years of the follow-up, n=53), and 70% at year 1. The table gives percentages only, with no counts in any of its 20 cells, and the counts cannot be recovered without back-calculating from a percentage. n_outcome_observed is left blank: the subgroup size is what the authors divided by, which belongs in reported_percentage_base, and the report never states for how many people income data were actually observed. | THE LARGER LOSS: no salary figure of any kind is printed for the 364-person working-age follow-up group. 53 + 159 = 212 of those 364 are in the two reported subgroups; the remaining 152 are never described, so even a complete set of counts for these two groups would not give a whole-cohort prevalence. | SUBGROUP SELECTION: both groups are defined by service contact during the LAST FIVE YEARS of the ten-year follow-up, a post-baseline variable the paper itself treats as an outcome ('different recovery paths'). They are subgroup arms of one cohort under D12.5, not cohorts, and they cannot enter the primary prevalence pool whatever their counts. | ANALYSIS-LEVEL SELECTION: the working-age group was formed by excluding 51 deceased, 10 untraceable and '22 retired persons' from 447. 'Retired' is nowhere defined. It most likely means old-age pensioners, since disability pension is separately tracked as a source of income WITHIN the analysed group (8% to 61%), which would make the restriction an age restriction and not an employment one; but the report does not say, and silence is not evidence of absence, so analysis_selection_status is `unclear` rather than `none`. | FOLLOW-UP: 'Year 1' is the year the psychosis diagnosis was set (Table 2 footnote a, p. 921), so year 10 is nine to ten years of elapsed time. 108 and 120 months both fall in the 108-months-and-above horizon, so the ambiguity has no effect on the band. | CONSTRUCT: 'salary from work on the labour market' establishes remuneration, so this is not `unclear`; it is coded paid_any because the register measure is any salary income with no threshold stated, though the report does not say whether subsidised or sheltered employment is included. | perc_employed_baseline records the year-1 (diagnosis-year) salary proportion of 70%, which is the only form in which the source prints it.
